front_blocks.md: Define **gravitational potential energy (GPE)**.

back_blocks.md: The energy an object has due to its **height** in a gravitational field.

back_blocks.md: If an object falls, energy is transferred **away** from its gravitational potential store.

front_blocks.md: State the equation for gravitational potential energy, defining each symbol.

back_blocks.md: $G P E = m \times g \times h$
Where *m* = mass (kg), *g* = gravitational field strength (N/kg), *h* = height (m), and GPE is in joules (J).

front_blocks.md: Define **kinetic energy**.

back_blocks.md: The amount of energy an object has as a result of its **mass** and **speed**.

front_blocks.md: State the equation for kinetic energy, defining each symbol.

back_blocks.md: $K E = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^{2}$
Where *m* = mass (kg), *v* = speed (m/s), and KE is in joules (J).

front_blocks.md: Does the amount of kinetic energy an object has depend on its direction of motion?

back_blocks.md: No. Kinetic energy depends only on **speed**, not direction, since only the magnitude of *v* is squared in the equation.

front_blocks.md: Define a **perfect energy transfer**.

back_blocks.md: An energy transfer in which there is **no wasted energy**; it is assumed when the wasted energy transfer is **negligible**, for example when air resistance is ignored.

front_blocks.md: A rollercoaster of mass 100 kg starts at a height of 15 m and reaches ground level, with frictional effects ignored (g = 10 N/kg). Calculate its maximum speed at ground level.

back_blocks.md: $Δ G P E = m \times g \times Δ h = 100 \times 10 \times 15 = 15000 \text{J}$
$Δ G P E = K E \text{(perfect transfer)}$
$v = \sqrt{\frac{2\timesKE}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\times15000}{100}} = 17 \text{m/s}$

cards.front_md: A rollercoaster of mass 100 kg starts at a height of 15 m and reaches ground level, with frictional effects ignored (g = 10 N/kg). Calculate its maximum speed at ground level.
cards.back_md:
$Δ G P E = m \times g \times Δ h = 100 \times 10 \times 15 = 15000 \text{J}$

$Δ G P E = K E \text{(perfect transfer)}$

$v = \sqrt{\frac{2\timesKE}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\times15000}{100}} = 17 \text{m/s}$

front_blocks.md: Define **power rating**.

back_blocks.md: The **power rating** of an appliance is the amount of energy it transfers per unit time, often given in watts (W), kilowatts (kW) or megawatts (MW). 1 kW = 1000 W and 1 MW = 1 000 000 W.

front_blocks.md: Two electric motors lift the same weight through the same height, but motor A does this in less time than motor B. Which motor has the greater power, and why?

back_blocks.md: **Motor A** has the greater power, because it transfers the same amount of energy (does the same work) in a **shorter time**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A higher power rating always means an appliance transfers more total energy than a lower-power one.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Power is the **rate** of energy transfer — the total energy transferred also depends on how long the appliance is used, so a lower-power appliance used for longer can transfer more total energy.

front_blocks.md: Describe the basic process by which most energy resources are used to generate electricity.

back_blocks.md: A **turbine** is turned (often by steam or moving water), which turns a **generator**, generating electricity that is transferred electrically to the National Grid.

front_blocks.md: In a fossil fuel power station, energy is transferred from the chemical store of the fuel to the **______** store of the water, which produces the steam that turns the turbine.

front_blocks.md: Describe the energy transfer chain when a wind turbine generates electricity for the National Grid.

back_blocks.md: Kinetic store of the **wind** → kinetic store of the **turbine** → kinetic store of the **generator** → transferred **electrically** to the National Grid.

Nuclear power stations generate electricity using steam to turn turbines, in a similar way to fossil fuel power stations.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

In both cases, water is heated to produce steam which turns a turbine connected to a generator — the difference is that the energy originates in the **nuclear store** of the fuel rather than its **chemical store**.

front_blocks.md: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of nuclear power as an energy resource.

back_blocks.md: Advantages include: reliable; produces large amounts of energy consistently; produces no pollution or CO<sub>2</sub>; large amounts of energy from small amounts of fuel.
Disadvantages include: produces radioactive waste that takes thousands of years to decay; expensive and slow to build and maintain; cannot respond quickly to changes in demand.

front_blocks.md: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using fossil fuels to generate electricity.

back_blocks.md: Advantage: **reliable** — can produce large amounts of energy consistently and respond to changes in demand.
Disadvantage: produces carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>), which contributes to global warming, and sulphur dioxide, which causes acid rain.

front_blocks.md: Wind power produces no pollution and has low running costs once built. Why is it still considered non-reliable?

back_blocks.md: Because it can only generate electricity when the **wind is blowing** (in a suitable direction) — it cannot produce energy on demand at any time.

front_blocks.md: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of tidal power.

back_blocks.md: Advantage: tides are very **predictable**, so energy can be produced at regular intervals.
Disadvantage: there are few suitable locations (estuaries), and it can harm aquatic life and disrupt shipping.
